meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been'?
meta.ogDescription: Wayne Gretzky gets the credit; the earliest citation quotes his father Walter Gretzky in January 1982. The popular wording is a smoothed paraphrase.

answer.label: Not originally Wayne Gretzky — his father, Walter Gretzky
answer.authorDates: 1938–2021 · Bell Canada repairman & Wayne Gretzky’s father and first coach
answer.sourceLine: The line is real, but it started as backyard coaching advice, not a Wayne Gretzky aphorism. The earliest citation quotation researcher Barry Popik records for the saying is a 27 January 1982 newspaper item quoting Walter Gretzky: “I always told him, ‘Skate to where the puck’s going to be, not to where it has been’” (Barry Popik ↗). Wayne did later use a first-person version himself — Popik’s earliest direct one is Newsday of 14 October 1990, “I go where the puck is going, not where it was” — so the popular boardroom form, “Skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been,” is a smoothed paraphrase of a line whose author was his dad.

source.excerpt: I always told him, “Skate to where the puck’s going to be, not to where it has been.”
trail: 1982 — the earliest citation Barry Popik records for the saying: Walter Gretzky, quoted 27 January 1982, “I always told him, ‘Skate to where the puck’s going to be, not to where it has been’” (Popik ↗). Popik also logs an earlier, differently worded 1972 newspaper note about anticipating where the puck is going, unconnected to the Gretzkys.

1983–1990 — the phrase crosses over and attaches to Wayne. Popik cites Computerworld of 12 December 1983 using the puck as a business metaphor; a Miami Herald TV column of 29 June 1984 relays Bill Moyers recounting Gretzky’s answer secondhand (“Someone asked the hockey star Wayne Gretzky … for the secret of his success”), not a Gretzky interview; the earliest direct first-person Gretzky citation in the file is Newsday of 14 October 1990, “I go where the puck is going, not where it was” (Popik ↗).

2000 — Walter says so himself. Popik’s file records a Fast Company Consultant Debunking Unit piece of 30 June 2000 in which Gordie Howe volunteers “That saying? It didn’t come from Wayne … It came from Wayne’s father, Walter,” and Walter Gretzky confirms he originated it, giving his own wording: “The quote is ‘Go to where the puck is going, not where it has been’” (Popik ↗).
Wikipedia’s biographies of both men credit the advice to Walter, delivered during backyard-rink sessions in Brantford (Walter Gretzky ↗; Wayne Gretzky ↗).
2013 — Legends Revealed examines the “Wayne coined it” claim and rates it False, naming Walter as the originator (Legends Revealed ↗).
source.excerptNote: Walter Gretzky, quoted in the Elgin Echo of 27 January 1982 — the earliest citation for the saying in Barry Popik’s file. Wayne Gretzky’s own first-person version, recorded in Newsday of 14 October 1990, runs: “I go where the puck is going, not where it was.”

source.rightsNote: This is a modern, twentieth-century line: the documented wordings come from newspaper and magazine reporting of 1982, 1990 and 2000, far later than the 1931 United States public-domain cutoff, so neither the quotations nor the articles carrying them are in the public domain. Quotle.info reproduces a single sentence for identification and comment only, and asserts no rights in it.

author.name: Walter Gretzky
author.heading: Who actually said it
author.metaLine: 1938–2021 · Bell Canada repairman, minor-hockey coach, father of Wayne Gretzky
author.bio: Walter Gretzky spent thirty-four years as an installer and repairman for Bell Canada and his winters flooding a backyard rink in Brantford, Ontario — the “Wally Coliseum” — where he drilled his son on anticipation rather than puck-chasing. The puck line was one of his standing coaching prompts. Wayne used it in the first person and it attached to his name; it was Gordie Howe and Walter himself who told Fast Company in June 2000 where it had actually come from. He became one of hockey’s best-known parents in his own right before his death in 2021.

misattribution.heading: Who really gets the credit
misattribution.intro: This is less a fabrication than a promotion: a father’s coaching line reassigned to his famous son, then trimmed for slide decks.

items.why: Wayne is documented using a first-person version — Popik’s earliest direct one is Newsday of 14 October 1990, “I go where the puck is going, not where it was” (a Miami Herald column of 29 June 1984 gets there first, but only as Bill Moyers recounting the answer secondhand) — while the earliest citation on file has his father saying it to him in 1982 (Barry Popik ↗). Legends Revealed rates the “Wayne coined it” claim False (Legends Revealed ↗).

items.who: “Skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been”
items.why: No documented transcription reads this way. Walter’s 1982 version is “Skate to where the puck’s going to be, not to where it has been”; Walter’s own preferred wording, given to Fast Company in June 2000, is “Go to where the puck is going, not where it has been”; Wayne’s 1990 version is “I go where the puck is going, not where it was” (Popik ↗). The circulating form welds “skate” to a clause none of them used.
Both are frequently cited as if they were quoting a Wayne Gretzky maxim; Popik files them as later users, including Jobs in January 2007 introducing the iPhone (Popik ↗).

misattribution.truthLine: Walter Gretzky said it first, in the documented record; Wayne said a version of it and made it famous; the wording on the slide is neither man’s exact sentence (Barry Popik ↗).

context.heading: How a hockey dad ended up in every pitch deck
lead: Almost nobody who quotes this line is talking about hockey. Barry Popik’s citation file shows the jump happening fast: by Computerworld of 12 December 1983 the puck had become a metaphor for telecommunications strategy, and the phrase has since been recycled by Warren Buffett and, in January 2007, by Steve Jobs introducing the iPhone (Popik ↗).

The irony is that the advice was never mystical. Walter Gretzky was teaching a kid on a backyard rink to stop chasing the puck — a coaching commonplace Popik finds in a differently worded 1972 note about anticipating where the puck is going. It became a slogan because it arrived attached to the most famous name in hockey.
detailsBody: Not everyone was impressed even in hockey circles: Popik’s file records U.S. Olympic coach Herb Brooks, in a June 2000 Fast Company feature, dryly observing that “You’d have to be a real idiot to skate to where the puck used to be.”

Business writers have made the same complaint since. Shawn Callahan’s 2006 essay argues organisations misread the line as a promise that the future can be predicted, when what elite players actually do is keep several options open (Anecdote ↗).
context.pull: The advice belonged to the dad. The fame belonged to the son.
